content: Eosin is a fluorescent acidic compound that binds to basic or positively charged compounds, such as proteins containing amino acid residues like arginine and lysine. This interaction results in the formation of salts, and eosin stains these structures a dark red or pink color. The staining effect is due to the chemical actions of bromine on fluorescein. Eosin is commonly used to stain proteins in the cytoplasm, as well as collagen and muscle fibers, for microscopic examination. Structures that readily take up eosin are referred to as eosinophilic. The term eosin is derived from the Ancient Greek word Eos, which means dawn, and is also the name of the Greek goddess of the dawn. There are two closely related compounds commonly referred to as eosin. The first, Eosin Y (also known as bromoeosine, bromo fluoresceic acid, or D&C Red No. 22), has a slightly yellowish hue. The second, Eosin B (also called Saffrosine, Eosin Scarlet, or Imperial Red), has a faint bluish tint. These two dyes are interchangeable, and their use depends on personal preference or tradition. Eosin Y is a tetrabromo derivative of fluorescein, while Eosin B is a dibromo dinitro derivative of fluorescein. In histology, eosin is most often used as a counterstain to hematoxylin in the hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining technique. H&E staining is one of the most widely used methods in histology. When tissues are stained with hematoxylin and eosin, the cytoplasm appears pink-orange, while the nuclei are stained dark blue or purple. Eosin also intensely stains red blood cells a bright red color. For staining purposes, Eosin Y is typically used in concentrations of 1% to 5% weight by volume, dissolved in either water or ethanol. To prevent mold growth in aqueous solutions, thymol is sometimes added. The addition of approximately 5% acetic acid to the solution can enhance the staining, producing a deeper red color in the tissue. Eosin is classified as a Group 3 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), indicating that it is not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans.
